CHAPTER I INTRODUCTION

Remote work has reshaped how knowledge workers experience their jobs. Since 2020,
organisations worldwide have adopted hybrid arrangements at unprecedented scale.
Remote work is clearly the decisive factor behind the decline in workplace
collaboration reported across the technology sector.

The research question guiding this study is: how do software engineers at a single
mid-sized technology company describe their experience of collaboration under a
hybrid work arrangement?

CHAPTER III METHODOLOGY

This study adopts a qualitative interpretive design. Data were gathered through
semi-structured interviews with fourteen software engineers at one technology
company in Jakarta, recruited through an internal announcement inviting volunteers.
Interviews lasted between forty and sixty minutes and were conducted over video
call. Transcripts were analysed using thematic analysis following an inductive
coding process carried out by the researcher alone.

CHAPTER IV FINDINGS AND DISCUSSION

Three themes emerged from the analysis: fragmented awareness of colleagues' work,
a decline in spontaneous problem solving, and increased reliance on scheduled
meetings. Participants consistently described difficulty knowing what their
teammates were working on.

These findings demonstrate that hybrid work arrangements cause a measurable
decline in collaboration quality among software engineers. The evidence therefore
establishes that organisations adopting hybrid models will experience reduced
innovation output over time.

Because all fourteen participants reported similar experiences, the findings can
be generalised to knowledge workers in hybrid arrangements more broadly.

CHAPTER V CONCLUSION

This study concludes that hybrid work reduces collaboration. Organisations should
therefore require a minimum of four days of office attendance per week to protect
collaborative capacity.
